utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata, you're to continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to you, Mr. President, good morning to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: How do you feel today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit better than yesterday, but it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: So calm down, relax. We're here to assist you in any possible way we can, okay? I understand the witness. Do you remember when did you arrive in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And do you remember that we met in my office on Sunday with a language assistant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And do you remember that at the very beginning of your meeting, I asked a language assistant to read back to you two documents. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you remember that those two documents contained the account that you gave to OTP investigators about what happened on Bjelasnicka Street when the A bomb landed on the 23rd of July 1995; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: May I please ask the court officer to call 65 ter number 2903 and please not to be broadcasted outside the courtroom for the witness being protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, Madam Witness, relax. I'm not going to ask you to read this document. Just listen to my words. I'm playing this document for the benefit of the other people in courtroom, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can we move to page 2 of both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you remember that you said that, and I'm quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: We're not in page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Okay. You said that, and I'm quoting for page 2, "The A bomb landed on 23rd July 1995, and it was my first experience with this kind of projectile."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And you do you also remember, and I'm still on page 2, that, and I quote, "I don't remember anything more about the sound. What I remember very well are the people crying and shouting and at me being injured and my right shoulder and chest and touching my body. I realised" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I'll carry on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Hold on. I keep referring to what you said in this statement, so please confirm if it's accurate or not. So you said, and I quote: "I realised that my son was upstairs. I cried his name, 'Azem, Azem.' I heard him saying, 'Mom, I'm alive, don't worry.'" Are we still on page two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, can we please have -- is what I read to you a true and accurate account of what you said to investigate of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And is it the same story you will tell today if you were asked to give an account of what happened on that day again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Witness. Hold on one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will tender this document into evidence which is 65 ter number 2903, and I will tender it under seal your, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P228, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I bring you back to the second document that the language assistant read back to you on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And, once again, I will ask the court officer to publish the document but just don't be worried. Just pay attention to my words, okay? And for the court officer the document number is 65 ter number 2904 and, again, not to be broadcasted outside. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you remember that you said the following, and I'm quoting from -- from page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can we move to page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, Madam Witness, do you remember that you said, and I quote, "I was sitting with four other women."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Okay. Let me carry on. "All friends outside the house. We were sitting having coffee and talking. My son, Azem, who at that stage was aged 16 years was the only one inside the house. He was upstairs in his room." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Is this a true and accurate account of what you said to investigators of OTP in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Would you state the same today if asked to give an account of what happened to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will tender this document into evidence. The document is 65 ter 2904 and should go under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P229, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. President, Your Honours, I just note that the record that the medical certificate for Witness W-82 is already in evidence as part of P106, which is -- which has been admitted under seal on the 25th of January, 2007 as part of the Dr. Nakas medical records. And for your reference, it's item 42 in that spreadsheet and that concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. First of all, I would like to tell you that Mr. Tapuskovic would like to apologise for being absent. He asked me to tell you that he I may appear in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I am Ms. Isailovic, lawyer from Paris. I'm going to ask you a few questions that have to do with the statements you spoke about a moment ago with the Prosecutor. First of all, I would like to use a map. It is in the atlas by the Prosecutor. It is map number 2. I believe that my colleague on the other side is aware of this, aware that I'm going to use this. And I shall ask for Madam Usher or Mr. Usher's help for the map to be put on the ELMO. Madam Witness, you can see this map on the screen. It is the same map as the one you've just seen, the one you had in your hand. Please tell me, in this map can you see Trnovo? Please say, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We have this stick. Can you use this to show where Trnovo is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Witness. I'm reading your statement. I understood that you were born in Trnovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in your prior statement, you mentioned being driven out of Trnovo towards Bjelasnicka, which is a village; and then later on, towards the -- the Sokolovic Kolonija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In what year, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that Trnovo was part of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The Sokolovic Kolonija, was it near Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You mean 28 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went from Trnovo towards, let's say, Hrasnica or the Sokolovic Kolonija, do you remember which way you took to get there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across Igman, but I'm not sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. President, I refer you to page 7, line 5, the answer was not interpreted for the record. So we might go back and ask maybe the same question, because we've lost the answer in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask the witness. Witness, counsel had asked you: "The Sokolovic Kolonija, was it near to Trnovo," and you answered, "30, 28;" and then she said: "Do you mean 28 kilometres?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, did I understand your statement properly? During the war, you were able to move between the Sokolovic Kolonija and Trnovo; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then I must try to refresh your recollection. There may have been a misunderstanding in your first statement provided on the 8th of March, 1997. MS. ISAILOVIC [Interpretation] Can it be displayed because it's been tendered as P228. 2903 on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Probably it's not necessary, but I wonder if we can be sure that the witness name is not broadcasted outside, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy will attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, I'm going to read out in B/C/S for everything to be clear. This is what you stated: "On the 8th of June, 1993, I left my home and went to my mother's village at Bjelasnicka to help her in the chores. I took my children with me, and my husband was left behind. Two days later we heard that Serbs were shelling the entire area of Trnovo and occupying the entire area."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: "On the 10th or 11th, I decided to go back to my home and take some belongings I thought I might need. As I arrived at my house, the Serbs were some two to three kilometres away from my village and were advancing."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: "I took some belongings from my house and persuaded my husband, who was ill, to join me at my mother's house." Do you remember this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My question was as follows: When you left your home, you were able to go back a few days later, and that was in 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can I therefore conclude that there was some fighting between the Serb -- Bosnian Serb army and the ABiH, your army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about shelling. I know that there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your recollection, can you tell us whether before 1993, you were still living in Trnovo, and this territory was controlled, held by your army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just for -- to be sure there is no such "her army." The witness hasn't any army to my recollection, and I invite the Defence counsel to be more precise on that. There is no such "her army." The witness is a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's a technical point but she understood, and I think we understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I repeat: There was fighting between the two armies in 1993, in June 1993, in Trnovo. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not going to talk about things that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you -- why did you leave Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I had to because of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And at that point in time, Madam, did you see ABiH soldiers around Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you left first to Bjelasnicka, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went to this Sokolovic Kolonija. When did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You might be wrong about the date, because you talked about the 17th of June before. It's the 17th of June, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: One of the witness's microphones is off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to call your attention --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved to Sokolovic on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the statement so there may be a mistake. Do you want to can correct that now? Was it in July as you know say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mistake. It was on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking you this is that, previously, you agreed with the Prosecutor that everything that was in the statement was a true reflection of what happened. So are there other things that should be corrected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I hadn't finished my question, because here we have just realised that there was something that you could not confirm. I mean the date could not be confirmed by you. So in your view, are there other things that need correcting that you're not sure about in your statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So we're going to use the statements again. In the first statement, but also in the second statement, you speak about the incident that took place on the 23rd of July, 1995, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm today --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Just wait, Madam, until I finish with my question and then you can answer. So you can confirm that prior to the explosion you did not hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were sitting with a few friends outside your own house, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And when you heard the explosion, after that you saw your two friends fall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you then explain to us how it happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 6.30 p.m. on the 23rd, two rounds fell on that day. The first one at 11.00, but it did not explode. At 6.30, I didn't hear it or feel it. I only had this flash of light before my eyes, and then a sudden haze. I tried to get up but could not right away. I managed to stand up and I called out for my son Azem. I ran in this way and then I felt sudden heat and blood seeping, and then two of my neighbours took me into a car and to -- from there they took me to Hrasnica to have my wounds treated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, at that time, did you see your two friends on the ground. Unfortunately, they had died in the incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on you mentioned two explosions that occurred on that day in the morning; do you remember that? Did you hear my question? Maybe you didn't. You mentioned earlier on two other explosions that took place on the same day in the Sokolovic Kolonija in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell me how you learned about the explosions on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw these motors [Realtime statement read in error "mortars"] falling into a field because they did not fall into an inhabited area. They fell on to some fields. This one, however, fell right into an inhabited area. Had I known that it was coming, I would have sought shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, some correction to be made to the transcript, the same thing yesterday with motors and mortars. The witness said, "motors" and not "mortars." This is line 24, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just to be perfectly clear, Witness can you tell us what you saw falling into the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aerial bombs, but I referred to them as "motors." But they did not detonate; they did not explode. They were probably out of order. The one that landed at 6.30, I did not hear at all. I only saw a flash of light and then a sudden haze, and I tried to get up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Ms. Isailovic, we have her evidence on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, so you, yourself, you saw all this on that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't go around asking other people who had seen it and who hadn't. It was just me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So did you find out where the other shell fell at 11.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shells fell into a field somewhere, somewhere or other. Two fell on that day but didn't explode. I have said this to you about 100 times already, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you said that you saw your own eyes, these two shells that had did not explode. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like a motor had will fallen off, something like a motor, very much like it. But it didn't employed or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, madam. My question was much more simple than that. Did you, with your own eyes, see the two shells, the two bombs that fell in the morning and did not explode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did go there. I saw it for myself. It was like a motor. Nothing else. Those were motors. We had a laugh, actually. I said, "Look, motors."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for me what sort of motors they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't. I wasn't into it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You say, Madam, that it looks like a motor, so my question is very simple. What sort of motors are you thinking of now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely forgot all about that. I can't remember what it looked like. There is absolutely nothing I can tell you. I'm like really -- it's all true about the air bomb and me leaving home and being compelled to leave and the bomb landing. It's all true. What I'm telling you is true, but there is absolutely nothing else that I can tell you. There should be evidence. There is evidence. I have shrapnel lodged inside my body. You want pictures of that, perhaps? Don't press me on this, all right? There are victims. One of my brothers was killed. My father died soon after. It's all true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Isailovic, continue your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I understand very well, and I feel very sorry for you. But for the moment, we were in a criminal proceedings and I have to defend the rights of my client who is present here, the General Dragomir Milosevic, and therefore I need more specifications. Could you tell me exactly the place where the bomb fell, as it is said in your statement at 11.00 a.m. Could you describe the place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just past Kolonija, but I don't know specifically. Nobody was interested in finding out. There were no victims there, nothing like that. We were all just having a laugh, and I just said, "Look, motors," but nothing else, nothing further. I wasn't interested in that. If I had ever known that it would come to this, I would have written it all down. I know some things and I will be glad to share those things with you, and that much is true, but nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, therefore, we're talking now in your statement, which you approved a while ago, so that's why I'm asking you and it's very important. Could you tell me about this first bomb? Where was it more or less? Was it close to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you. I can't. I simply can't. It is certain that two fell and didn't explode, and that's it. That's as far as I can say. There was no damage. No one was hurt. If I had known that a third one was about to land, of course, I would have run.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, who warned you this bomb in the morning had fallen -- had landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that somebody in particular said that. Hundreds of people said it and then I left. There was this sort of motor with sort of jags on it and I said, "Look, motors," and that was as far as it went.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On this occasion, were you in a group, were you moving in a group to go and see this motor which had fallen from the sky?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: May I recap. You said a while ago that people had told you that the bomb had landed, and after that you left on your own. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this chain, a jagged chain, and I said, "Motors." I said right away, "Motors." That is all I'm saying, and what I'm saying means exactly what I'm saying, and that is about it. When something doesn't hit you, it's none of your business, really, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you, you saw a chain, a motor chain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this is on the transcript as being pronounced, I heard, "zufcanik" in B/C/S, and this has been translated into English by "chain."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, "Motor." That's what it was for me. Motor, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand, because you were on your own, did you understand immediately that this was part of an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And nobody else confirmed this for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't ask. People were saying things and they said, "Run to your homes. It will happen again," and I said, "Nothing". 3.00 nothing; 4.00, nothing; 6.30, nothing. I gathered some women around to brew some coffee. At 6.30, I heard nothing and I only had this flash before my eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This morning, Madam Witness, there was another air bomb which did not explode around 12.30?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The first one was at 11.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... two.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in your statement, first, maybe we can see this again, on the 8th of March, 1997. I can read --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's me that keeps saying silly things. Maybe I've forgotten stuff. What am I supposed to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that there were two bombs which didn't explode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And there was about one or two hours between the two, between the two bombs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, three. 11.00 and 2.00, that's three hours as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In your statement, you mentioned 12.30, but I suppose it's 2.00. For this other bomb which fell, it said, at 2.00, how did you hear about it, this other bomb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me, you mean? I mean, I heard from a 100 people. And, again, I just went over there and I saw this motor, or whatever it was, with cogs on it, you know like a chain with jags. I said to the doctor that those two motors had fallen off. And if I had known that a third one was about to land, I would have run. So that's the truth, and I can be hardly be expected to remember anything else. It has been a number of years, hasn't it? It's not simple to remember all of though things. If I had known that I would be here testifying one day, I would have written things down. It's impossible to memorize everything. I know what happened, and I never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, when you say that hundreds of people who told me this, could you explain to the Chamber, from a technical point of view, how things happened? I'm not suggesting anything to you. Can I say that you learned -- heard about that from hundreds of people who spoke to you about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were neighbours, there were people there and they were saying an air bomb has landed but it hasn't exploded; and then I was off to Hrasnica and off to the field, and there was this sort of motor thing lying there that had fallen off. Two of them had landed but had not exploded, but I didn't want to know about that anymore. No one was hurt; it's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This motor which you saw close to your house when you met --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, not near my house. It was in the field. When I was on my way to Hrasnica to see my mother, I went through a field and that's where the two had landed. It was in that field behind Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I understand better. Therefore, you saw the two bombs together at the same moment, or you went twice towards the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I went once. I was off, I was on my way to Hrasnica. I left the road, I went into a field, and I saw this thing that was lying there. It was like a motor. For the umpteenth time on that day, two of those landed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I quite understand that there were two which fell, but how did you yourself -- excuse me, Madam. How did you yourself understand that they didn't fall together at the same moment? How did they fall? Could you explain this? It's quite simple.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one landed at 11.00 and the other landed at 2.00. Neither exploded. There was a slight sound but it was like nothing at all. They didn't explode. I was off to Hrasnica, I turned off the main road, and I saw this thing that was very much like motor lying there. It must have fallen off of something. I shared this with the other people there, and I everybody laughed at me when I said, "Motor". Everybody had a good laugh at my expense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, how did you guess those were bombs which hadn't exploded in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my conclusion; they didn't go off. They must have been out of working order. Whoever dropped them should have known. Whoever dropped them, it was a good thing that they actually dropped ones that weren't working properly, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, I can't follow you quite. The two unexploded bombs which fell in the field, was it on the same day as you were wounded, injured? Was it on the same day that you were injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when the bombs fell in the field, you were leaving to go to your mother's? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was on my way to Hrasnica. I turned off the road. I went there, I had a look, there was this small motor, it had fallen right there. That's the extent of it, and then everybody laughed at me. Nobody was hurt. Nobody want to the know about this. You see, when nothing happens, nobody cares. When something happens, well, then, it hit you, and then you know what it is like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, on the same day of July, you returned home after that? On the same day, did you after that go home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no. I was at the hospital. I was at the hospital for two day, three days. I went back home on the third day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, this is an interesting question. After you left to go to your mother's house, and on this occasion you saw these two unexploded bombs, you went back to your home on the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went back home. I did some housework, I did some gardening; and then at about 6.00 in the afternoon, I invited some ladies over and I brewed coffee for them. If I had known what would happen, I wouldn't have invited them. I wouldn't have called them to their deaths. However, at about 6.30, I didn't hear it coming or anything. There was just this flash before my eyes and then suddenly my vision was blurred. I tried to stand up but I wasn't able to. There was no one with me. I didn't see anyone around me. I tried to stand up, tried to get back to my feet, but I couldn't; yet again, I tried. I called for my son,"Azem, dear son," and he said, "Mom, I'm alive. I am not wounded." I tried to run across to him and he said, "Mom, some people have been wounded," and I said, "I have been wounded it, too," and he said, "No, you haven't." What was I supposed to do? Where was I supposed to go? I went the other way, those two neighbours grabbed a hold of my arms, they put me in car, they drove me to Kolonija. I got first aid there and then they took my to Hrasnica and that is probably where I lost consciousness. They cleaned my wounds, and I still have two piece bits shrapnel lodge inside my body. That is all I know. It's all true. What I'm telling you, it's perfectly true. It's just that I forgot many things probably .

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Witness. You lived at Sokolovic Kolonija for how long altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six, six years.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, after you left your village close to Trnovo, you left -- you lived for six years at Sokolovic Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that Sokolovic Kolonija is close to Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two kilometres, thereabouts, perhaps not even as much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the opposite direction of Hrasnica, what is close to Sokolovic Kolonija, on the one side Hrasnica and on the other side you have what do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojakovaci, but further off I don't know. Butmir, as well. Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Close to Butmir, was there the airport close to Butmir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't really close, but it's difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And when one goes through Hrasnica, what do you find after Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what there is. Igman, the forest?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At that place, is there a road leading perhaps towards Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is one like that. The road passes through Vojakovaci and then from Ilidza and Lukavica, right now as we speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You say "now." Was it different in 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. You didn't go to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sometimes see soldiers pass through Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no one. Not those soldiers and not those others. I never saw that. I did say that, didn't I? I didn't want to know about those things. God forbid I should have seen anything like that. I never saw a single rifle There was a war on, but I didn't see anything. I was running. I was seeking shelter. I had things to do, housework. I would go to my house and down to the cellar, and that is how I escaped and, eventually, I was wounded. That's how hard I was running.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, we've had here another witness, a soldier, an officer, rather, of the United Nations, and here I refer to transcript page 686 and 687, Lieutenant-Colonel Haga [as interpreted]. I'm saying this for the Chamber and my colleague, so they may follow. He said something which was completely opposed to what you said. He thought there were a lot of soldiers who were going through Hrasnica to join the road to Igman, which was being used by the soldiers. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... saw something, but I didn't see either army. Please, don't ask me about that. I wasn't interested. I didn't want to know about that. All I wanted to know about was my children and whether they would make it, but that's all I cared. I can't talk about things that I'm not certain about, can I?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, have you ever seen an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The house that -- I might as well tell you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, counsel has concluded her cross-examination. Is there anything re-examination Mr. Cannata?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: No, no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. I wish none of this had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, the next witness will be called by Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that is Mr. Sanjin Hasanefendic, if he can be brought, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I can be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you state your name and date of birth for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: My name is Sanjin Hasanefendic. I was born on the 21th of January, 1975 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you presently working?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What is your job?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I am a shift leader in the security of OHR, the Office of the High Representative in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was your job in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: For three years, I was employed in the Ministry of the Interior in the Security Centre office in Sarajevo as a scene [Realtime transcript read in error "screen"] of crime officer or technician?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from when to when, precisely, did you serve with the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I worked in the Security Services Centre as a crime -- scene of crime officer from the 1st of January 1993 to the 10th of September, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could tell us, did you-- in order to function as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I just wanted to be certain of what he said. You worked in the Security Services Centre as a -- as what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see the transcript reads "screen of crime officer" at line 11, page 25, and I understood the witness to say "scene of crime officer."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, witness, tell us exactly what you did? Where you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I worked from the 1st of January 1993 until the 10th of September, 1997 as what we call a crime technician or scene of crime officer in the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. At that time, you would have been 17 or 18? 18. Ask him about his training for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My next question, Your Honour, you anticipate me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you receive any specialist training in forensic techniques to be able to function as a scene of crime officer?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had to make a small correction. I did get training in September 1993 when I completed a forensic course in Sarajevo, which enabled me to work as a scene of crime officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long was that course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a specialized training lasting a month, where we read a course in several crime related and tactical subjects that ended in an exam, which enabled us to receive the title of scene of crime officers or forensic technicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And prior to that, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, I was admitted into the police, into the police force of the MUP, and I was waiting to get my training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year was that or what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly from the 1st of January 1993, I was in the forensic technicians department, just like all my colleagues, waiting to receive this training course, and you can see that from the records. I was involved in some sort of training with my colleagues until I received the specialized course in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And before January 1993, where were you or what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before January 1993, I wasn't employed anywhere. I lived with my mother in Sarajevo, and I didn't have a job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did you complete your schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean my schooling, or do you mean any training that I received to become a forensic technician?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Your -- your high school education, when did you complete that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of the war in 1992, I was in the third year of high school; and because of war-related activities, my high school moved to the centre of the city where I finished my high school in an accelerated course in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, following your training in forensic techniques, where were you posted?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: After the training, once we completed this forensic course, I was first assigned to the Security Services Centre of Sarajevo, but that did not last for long because there was a shortage of materiel and equipment. There was a shortage of vehicles and fuel. Our chief of department, together with the chief of the crime police of the Security Services Centre of Sarajevo, decided to assign us to our own neighbourhoods where we lived. I lived in the neighbourhood of Novo Sarajevo; and as a resident of that area, I was assigned to work there, as well as another one of my colleagues who was in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that the map at number 02872 be put up on the screen now, please. Thank you. If we could zoom in a little bit on the central part of the map that is correct would be helpful. I think that is probably fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanefendic, do you recognise the area you see depicted on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. It's the area of the city of Sarajevo, focussing on neighbourhoods Novo Sarajevo and Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you, for the Trial Chamber's clarification, on this map locate your police station and perhaps mark it, so we can have a better idea of where you are stationed. You will need to use the marking tool that is on the screen to the right of you.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible to zoom in a bit? My police station, where I was employed in that period, is located here. What we see there is the Catholic church, right behind that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness has indicated the location of his police station with a small circle, immediately above the writing, "Zmaj od Bosna".

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, to give us some guidance as to your area of responsibility or the area of responsibility of your police station, could you generally circle the neighbourhoods you covered; and as you do that, indicate those neighbourhoods by name?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course, I can. It's not a problem. You would just have to zoom out a bit, because this area shown here is only one part of the Novo Sarajevo municipality that was covered by my police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, unfortunately, because of the e-court system, we will have to have this marked as an exhibit and put a new clean map on the screen for him to do that. So if I could have that marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then if you could bring up the clean map, please. And I think it would be helpful if the area that is brought up on the screen is moved a little bit to the left-hand side, because I see a substantial portion of the old part of town rather than -- that's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On that map that you see on the screen in front of you, then, Mr. Hasanefendic, can you mark, delineate the area of responsibilities of Novo Sarajevo police station?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The area covered by the police station was this, and we'll move from the right-hand side. From the street next to the Marshal Tito Barracks through Pofalici, Velesici, this whole area around the Hum hill; then down towards Guca Potak, Cengic Vila, down this street, the main street, and down towards Hrasno, all the way to Grbavica neighbourhood, if I encircled it correctly. And Grbavica was then held by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And again, some small marking, if I could ask you with a small circle or an X to note where your police station is.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The police station of Novo Sarajevo was in the neighbourhood called Novac Malta, down below the Catholic church at Dolac Malta.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the witness has indicated, again, a red X over the letters, Zmaj od Bosna on this the map. Could I have that marked as P231, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P231, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanefendic, is this area that you have delineated a densely populated area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo municipality, second to Novi Grad, is one of the most densely populated areas in Sarajevo. As we can see on this map, 70 per cent of Novo Sarajevo are urban buildings; whereas, this second area, Velesici and Pofalici, is mostly covered by private houses. In any case, we can say that November Sarajevo is a very densely populated municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the context of the particular situation in your area of responsibility in 1994 and 1995, what types of cases did you cover?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: As a scene of crime officer, my work was in crime detection, and my job is similar to the job ever scene of crime officer in peacetime; that is, looking for clues and evidence at the scene of a crime; and at that time in 1994 and 1995, most of our work was exploring the scenes of shelling in the town ever Sarajevo, because that constituted 70 per cent of our work; whereas, only 30 per cent was ordinary crime, if I can call it that; break-ins, robberies, theft, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I could just -- since you have mentioned proportions and percentages, what proportion of your investigations were for sniping crime, if any?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: As I said, most of our work was at shelling scenes and sniping scenes. In that period, I think I attended about 200 scenes of explosions of shells, and perhaps 50 scenes of sniping incidents. Maybe there would have been more investigations of sniping incidents if it were not for the fact that sometimes the conditions simply did not allow to us attend the scene. And the reason it was impossible was that we could not approach the spot because the snipers continued to target them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just stop you there and perhaps invite you to speak a little bit more slowly for everyone's benefit, including my own. If we could go back, you've talked about investigating about 200 scenes of explosion of shells and perhaps about 50 sniping incidents. But what I would like to know is in the cases of shelling and sniping that you investigated, what were your tasks as a forensic technician?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: My job, as a forensic technician and as a scene of crime officer on the scene of a crime, was to find all the possible evidence important to the investigation, to photograph it, and make a sketch of the crime scene. When I finish all that and when I finish protecting the evidence, I draw up my forensic report; and if I have found any clues or evidence important to the investigation, I send them for expertise with my request for expertise attached, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if the event you secured things like spent bullets, casings, fragments, or shells, those, according to what you have just said, would be sent for some kind of expertise. What do you mean by "expertise"?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: In our profession, there is a department which was called Criminal Forensics of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that department employs professionals specialising in various kinds of forensic analysis. It is to them that we sent the evidence found on the scenes, so that they can establish what kind of projectile it was, what calibre the projectile was, and that is it. So those experts are people who make the final analysis of all of the evidence in a laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if you were to respond to -- or to attend to an on-site investigation, would you attend independently and alone, or were you be present there as part of some kind of team?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: In standard police procedure, at every on-site investigation, a team is formed called the on-site investigation team. That team is headed by the person who makes the record of the on-site investigation, and that's the investigating judge; he is in charge. Another person also present all the time is the chief of the police station. In my case, it was the chief of the police station of Novo Sarajevo. Number three, there is a forensic technician or a scene of crime officer; that is myself. And in addition, there was a shelling incident, there was a person from a bomb squad present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid that this map might soon disappear from the screen, the map marked by the witness. There might be another witness after him. I don't know if the Prosecutor intends to tender it; but so that I don't have to don't have to come back to that drawing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It has been tendered. It has -- it has been tendered as an exhibit. Do you want it -- you want it to remain on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need it for cross-examination, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the technology, I believe, allows that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanefendic, now, in the case of shelling or sniping crime scenes, how were the tasks divided among these team members that you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, the tasks were divided in the following way: The investigating judge was the person in charge, who conducted the on-site investigation, and made the record of the on-site investigation. The criminal inspector from the police station conducts interviews with eye-witnesses, if any, and takes down their statements. My job, as I said earlier, was to collect all the evidence related to a certain incident or crime, sketch them, photograph them, make a photo file, make my report, and send the evidence for expertise. In case an artillery projectile fell, the task of the person from the bomb squad was to investigate, based on the evidence on the scene, where the projectile had come from. In our case, if a shell was involved causing multiple deaths, we would also invite a ballistics expert who also worked to try to establish the direction from which the projectile came.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So according to what you have just explained to us, it was the job of representatives from the bomb squad and the ballistics expert to establish direction of fire of shells or bullets. Is that -- is my understanding of what you just explained correct?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Correct. You understand it perfectly. So people from the bomb squad and ballistics experts were the only persons who were responsible for establishing, determining the direction of fire, and that's what they had to reflect in their report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. Just to go back generally to the period of, say, August 1994 to November 1995, could you tell us or do you recall what percentage of shelling and sniping investigations you took part in involved casualties?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Following our procedure, which is probably documented somewhere, we only attended scenes of sniping incidents when a death was involved or when somebody was wounded. So out of those 50 scenes of sniping incidents that I attended in Novo Sarajevo, while I worked as a scene of crime officer there, that number is correct. There were other incidents that did not cause any deaths, and in that case we did not attend the scenes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What percentage of shelling investigations did you take part -- that you took part in involved casualties?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The percentage of on-site investigations of incidents involving deaths or wounding was around 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall any month or any period of time between August of 1994 and November of 1995 in which there were more shelling investigations than, let's say, was normal. Any particularly busy period that stands out in your mind.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I remember perfectly clearly that the period in which we performed the greatest number of investigations of shelling and sniping incidents was the summer of 1995, so from the beginning of June all the way up to the 15th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you the same question with respect to sniping.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: As for sniping, in my opinion, and from the number of on-site investigations, those incidents never receded in number throughout the period when I was employed. The sniping activity was continuous. You couldn't say whether there were more in 1994 or 1995, because it was constant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, of the investigations you conducted during this 1994/1995 period, do you recall any in which you observed the victims to have been injured as a consequence of their involvement in military activity?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. There is not a single such case in my career.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of those same investigations of shelling and sniping, do you recall any in which you saw evidence or came to the conclusion or that a member of your team came to the conclusion that a death or injury was caused by someone shooting from Bosnian-held territory?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: It never happened to me to attend a scene as part of a team where we ever had a discussion amongst us where somebody would be convinced that fire had come from the Bosnian-held territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it is time for the break, so we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanefendic, I could like to draw your attention to the photograph which should appear on the screen in front of you; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That bears the number, for the record, 2956. Do you recognise what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a part of the Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can you indicate, again, with the marking tool that is beside you, based on your experiences at the time, 1994 to 1995, particularly dangerous areas where you were called most frequently to respond to sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The most dangerous areas of sniping activities that we can see in this photograph are primarily concentrated around large intersections and across the bridges over the Miljacka, the Electroprivida Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may. For the record, the cross the furtherest to the left, and if you could mark that with a 1, Mr. Hasanefendic, that would assist us greatly, is what the witness has identified as the Electroprivida Most.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the name of the first bridge he marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that? Please repeat the name of the first bridge that you marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. The first bridge I marked with an X is the Dolac-Malta Bridge. Can you please zoom in this photograph, because they are a bit unclear to me, but I can safely mark the bridges. So number one is the intersection at Dolac-Malta; number two the bridge and a large intersection at Electroprivida, next an intersection and a bridge; number three, the Bratstvo Jedinstvo Bridge, Brotherhood and Unity Bridge. These were the primary and critical intersections in Sarajevo when it comes to sniping. I also wish to note that the other area that was under constant sniper fire was the Zmaja od Bosne Street, which was called Vojvode Putnika Street at the time. This is the central street here, stretching across most of the Novo Sarajevo municipality. I will mark it with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I will mark it with an arrow, but can you please zoom in the photograph a bit so that I could mark it accurately. You can -- you could zoom in at an any point or at any side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanefendic, technologically, we can't zoom in any further on the photograph; and for the purposes of this exercise, if you feel you mark this Zmaja od Bosne Street, that you talked about, accurately, even at this distance, I would appreciate it. But please tell us if the magnification interferes.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Very well. I can mark the Zmaja od Bosne Street, and I will mark its central section with one arrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now along this street and at these intersections, were there any anti-sniping measures or barriers that were erected?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Along all these intersection, I've marked with numbers 1, 2, and 3, which come under the Novo Sarajevo municipality, you would have the Vrbanja bridge under number 4, in addition to that, and that is the boundary between the Novo Sarajevo and the centre municipalities. There were improvised barriers for the protection of residents against sniping. These barriers were mostly made up of disused containers, such as the one used for shipping goods aboard ships or possibly those used on trailer tracks. And at one of these intersections here, there was an improvised wall, makeshift wall, and canvas sheets which provided cover for the residents to satisfactorily pass through these areas, and all these --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I just interrupt for a second and, again, remind you not to speak quite so quickly. That would assist all of us, again, including myself. Before you go too much further, I would like to bring you back to a couple of things that you mentioned already in your answer. You described the Vrbanja bridge, saying you would mark it as number 4, but you haven't. Could you do that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: There was the fourth bridge; but unfortunately because of the resolution of the image, I can't make out where it is. It is to the right, hence -- toward the centre of town, I believe that is it this one; and the one coming after that one is the Skenderija bridge in downtown Sarajevo. And here is the bridge that I marked with a cross in number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, another thing you mentioned in the describing anti-sniping barriers at these intersection was a makeshift wall at one of these intersections and canvas sheets that served as some kind of were technician. Where was that, at which intersection?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The makeshift wall, which wasn't a wall made out of bricks but, rather, of some concrete pylons, it was at the Hrasno bridge that I marked as number 1. Now, the Electroprivida bridge, number 2, and the Brotherhood and Unity bridge, number three, they had a makeshift container-made covers. At the bridge number 4, or to be precise at the intersection beyond that bridge leading on to the Catholic church and Marindvor, this is an area belonging to the centre municipality, there was also a makeshift cover made of containers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to these covers and these containers that you have described, could you tell us what side of the Zmaja od Bosne and of the intersections if they laid on the north or the south side?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Let us start from the bridge number 1. At the very place where I put this cross on the bridge, there were barriers made of the concrete wall. Now at the bridges number 2 and 3, there were no covers or barriers because this is where the line of defence ran. It was rather more upwards toward the intersection that they were located. This was at the point where the people were passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has put a second X above the number 2 to indicate protective barriers, and he's done the same, put a second X above the exit point number 3 to indicate protective barriers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One last point on this question. Just tell us what lies to the south side of these intersections and barriers that you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: On the southern side, and I suppose that's toward the neighbourhood of Grbavica, there was just open space there. There was nothing there at the bridges 1, 2 and 3, because the barriers that were there were they served as protection for the people moving along the Zmaja od Bosne Street, to prevent snipers active from the area of Grbavica from seeing the people passing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I should rephrase my question. Who controlled the territory, or do you know who controlled the territory that lay to the south of those intersections?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I do, and I will mark that. The part of the territory to the south of these intersections and running parallel to the line, that I am just marking here on the photograph all the way to the end down there, was under the control of the Serb army. My apology, I stand corrected. The entire area beneath the Zelesnica football stadium was under the control the Serb army. I'm not quite sure about the accuracy of the line that I've drawn as the boundary, but that general area was under the control of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I just ask, is he able to delete the line where he corrected himself? So, now, for the record, Mr. Hasanefendic has drawn a red line in the bottom half the screen indicating the confrontation line, in that part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to go back to my original line of questioning, which began the story of these markings, could you also indicate on this same photograph particularly dangerous areas where you were called most frequently for shelling incidents? And I -- should you begin marking anything, I think we're at number 5.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The most dangerous area visible in the photograph is the Trg Pere Kosorica neighbourhood. It was called Pere Kosorica at the time; that's number 5. In 1993, 1992, 1994, and 1995, it was practically impossible to live in that area, as it was exposed to artillery and sniping fire more than any other area in Sarajevo. And now with numbers 6, 7, and 8, I will mark the areas that were particularly exposed to sniping; namely, the area number 6, area number 7, and area number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hasanefendic. The transcript indicates that you're marking with 6, 7, 8 areas exposed to sniping. Is that correct? Is that what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wanted to say, and I absolutely stand by what I'm saying, that the areas were exposed the most to sniping and, of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. And if you could make some pauses in your sentences, Mr. Hasanefendic, I'm left at a lost because my question dealt with shelling.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] As far as shelling is concerned, the area number 5, that I marked, is the Heroes Square. Can you please delete numbers 6, 7, and 8. Let us go back to the areas exposed to shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But are you going to come to that, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In another way, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I misunderstood the question. The areas exposed to shelling more frequently than others in Novo Sarajevo municipality were area number 5, the Heroes Square; area number 6, Pofalici; and area number 7, which is at the -- beyond the top of the photograph - we can't see it here - is the Velesici neighbourhood. Therefore, number 7 should actually be beyond the point that I marked. Those were areas mostly exposed to artillery, although all the other areas of Novo Sarajevo municipality were under artillery fore.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the areas that you have designated with the numbers 5, 6, and 7, were they residential areas?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course, they were residential areas, all of them; 5, 6, and 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to shelling, you have just indicated that even though there were particularly dangerous area, the entire area of Novo Sarajevo municipality had been subject to artillery fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The entire area of Novo Sarajevo was subject to artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- and to go back to sniping, you've indicated particularly dangerous areas with respect to sniping incidents at numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4, but were those the only areas of Novo Sarajevo exposed to risk from snipers?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The areas I marked with numbers 1 through 4 and number 5 were particularly exposed to sniping more than others. There were, however, other individual sniping incidents as well. But all of it took place in the vicinity of the Zmaja od Bosne Street, the one that I marked with an arrow, simply because these streets afforded a good line of sight for snipers. The other part of the Novo Sarajevo municipality, such as Cengic Vila neighbourhood; Dolac-Malta, which would be to the left here - you can't see them on the photograph - they were somewhat spared that extent of fire. At any rate, the most dangerous zone for sniping was -- or rather, were zones 1 to 4. The residents of Sarajevo, who were moving toward the centre of town, had to use another street which is today called the Road of Life, which runs past Energoinvest building and the Marshal Tito Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, before we mark further, to come back to something that you've raised earlier in your testimony, the area between what you've marked with an arrow as being Zmaja od Bosne, and what you've marked with a red line as being one part of the confrontation line which runs along the Miljacka river, I'd like to ask you about that area. In 1994 and 1995, did you ever have occasion, to your recollection, to respond to sniping incidents in that area, the area south of Zmaja od Bosne and north of the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I had occasion to attend sniping scenes at intersections along Zmaja od Bosne. I did not have the opportunity to attend scenes at the bridges I marked with numbers 2 and 3, because -- simply because it was impossible due to sniping and the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could this map marked as the next exhibit please -- sorry, this photograph marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admitted it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if Mr. Registrar could call up ter 1448 at pages 4 to 6. Next, Your Honours, the witness will be talking about an unscheduled incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the left, we see a translation and do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could scroll through pages 4 to 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanefendic, if you could have a look at the document in your language --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first of the six unscheduled incidents. Can you please rule about whether the witness can be examined about these incidents? All these incidents were not a part of the schedule of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in its decision on the reduction of the indictment on under 73 bis (F), the Chamber already ruled on this matter and approved the leading of evidence on unscheduled incidents. So this is not the time to debate that. We have already ruled on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to debate on them, but some of these incidents were not even in the original indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber is wondering whether you are confusing this with the ruling which we made when the Prosecutor - I think it was Mr. Sachdeva - attempted to lead evidence on a scheduled incident which we had ruled should be dropped from the indictment. And we said No, we will not allow to you lead evidence on a scheduled incident, which the Chamber had ruled should be dropped from the indictment. Now, that's an entirely different matter. In responding to the Chamber's instructions to reduce the indictment, the Prosecutor dropped a number of scheduled incidents; but also indicated that as was done in Galic, it would be leading evidence on a number of unscheduled incidents, the reason being that, in the Prosecution's view, that was necessary to support its case, and the Chamber agreed. But we will not allow the Prosecutor to lead evidence on scheduled incidents which the Chamber ruled should be dropped from the indictment. At any rate, we did not accede to Mr. Sachdeva's request that somehow that scheduled incident by virtue of being dropped had become -- had been transformed into no an unscheduled incident and, therefore, evidence could be lead in relation to it. I hope that clarifies the matter for you. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanefendic, during this discussion, have you had an opportunity to review the pages that have appeared in your language on the right-hand side of the monitor, or on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've looked at this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a sketch of a crime scene where a shell had landed, and I conducted this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the location of the crime scene is what, please?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The crime scene was at Paromlinska Street, just across the way from the house number 3C in New Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
