utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the investigating judge called at all it to this incident?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. His assistance was required. He features in the report, but I now don't recollect very clearly. In such cases, investigating judges usually authorise the police inspector to create the report, and they did not come with us into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, we don't have the reports and opinions and findings of the most competent people; namely, investigating judges.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that. My job was something different, to create my own forensic report, a sketch, photo file, and a request for expertise. The forensics department, where I work, has nothing to do with the rest of the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you state that as far you know the bomb flew very slowly. Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain how the projectile like that could have torn through the entire building length-wise? It's quite a broad building. How could it with penetrated all the way through? Did you establish that, and how did you establish that such a thing was possible?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: We did establish that to have been a possibility. The building had offices either side of the central staircase, so it wasn't particularly wide, the way I remember it. The projectile went off inside the building between the second and third floors near the staircase, not more than a metre from the actual window. Therefore, the projectile did not tear through the entire building. It went off inside, and its explosive charge caused the damage to the building that is depicted in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I could show you more photographs of that building. I'm putting it to that you based on the photographs I have seen, and the Chamber is in possession of those photographs, I'm putting it to you that building was hit by who knows how many different projectiles. Any comment, sir?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. First of all, there is inaccurate, your suggestion that it was hit by several projectiles. It was only hit by one, by a single projectile, by a modified air bomb of which we found bits and pieces, even some of the fins and the engine of the little of the little motor that propelled this modified air bomb. I'm not an expert myself. I'm not sure how much explosive it contained, but it was probably a powerful charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, in those days, there were not constant ongoing clashes between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The New Sarajevo municipality was being shelled heavily at the time. There were no particular clashes in my own area where I worked, but I can't speak about any other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps say whether the BiH army, too, fired back?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: You see, I was a scene of crime officer, a member of the police. I never even carried weapons throughout the war. That was the kind of work I did. That was my job. I can hardly comment on anything to do with BH army activity or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling me that throughout the war, being a police officer and having such a tough job, you never carried a weapon. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I never carried a weapon at all. Five of my colleagues can confirm that for you. I had signed for a pistol that I was entitled to in the line of duty, but I kept it at home. None of us needed one actually. The inspector was carrying a pistol, but that was all he was carrying. The bomb squad person need no weapon, and I need he had no weapon myself. That was the sort of job we had. I had to actually sign for a pistol, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 00186, please, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown page 4 by the Prosecutor. It's an Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please run that up on our screens. "Official Note dated the 25th of August."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The second-to-last paragraph, it's a huge one. It says: "Probably fired from south-west, which coincides with the positions held by the Serbian army, the army of Republika Srpska, at the Rajlovac PZT." Where is Rajlovac relative to the building that was hit?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Relative to the building? Rajlovac is to the west, south-west, possibly. Rajlovac as a general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say, "tore through glass," and I won't be reading on. I'm just quoting the relevant portion that I will base my question on. "At the time of the explosion, the man who came to grief who was inside a motor vehicle accident in a Golf car and the registration plate number from Sarajevo, and this vehicle was parked outside the building next to the Gol restaurant at Zmaja od Bosne, number 66. "The person that sustained injuries to the chest. He got out of the car and fell on the ground next to the restaurant, where citizens gathered to help him, that they put him in an unidentified car and took him to the hospital. However, he succumbed to his wounds on the way to the hospital, while Alija Muharemovic was merely injured." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. That's what it says, and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs at the scene? I mean where this man fell to the ground, did you see any blood mark there is?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did photograph the vehicle, the Golf vehicle. I did photograph the scene, the site where he was injured; and as far as I remember, I photographed the blood marks that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking. He got out of the car, he crossed a certain distance, he fell down, and other people picked him up. I'm asking you, did you photograph the blood marks on the spot where this unfortunate man fell down?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think so. It's been a long time since I last went through the photo files, but I must have because he didn't fall down that far away. The place where he eventually fell down was quite near the car, the Golf car. I should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have the photographs of that car and the blood marks in the car that you found, right?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But there's no way I could know where the car was, and that's why I can't ask you that, can I? What I'm asking you is if we look at these photo files, why is there no solid evidence -- I mean no photograph to show blood marks on the spot where the man fell down?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Simply because --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with any malicious intent, but I hear the parties speaking to one another without any pause in between, and it-- I'm suffering and I'm sure other people are trying to follow what is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I must ask both the witness and counsel to observe a pause between question and answer, don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, there is no photograph here of the actual place where this man, who had previously got out of the car, fell down. No blood marks were photographed. Can you explain why? Why did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I can't explain why that wasn't done. I did take the photographs. I photographed the vehicle in which the man had been, the man who eventually you succumbed. Why did we not photograph the place where he fell down is really not something that I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting it to that you that you he was not killed on this spot where you say he was?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: And I'm putting it to you -- I'm putting it to you that he was, and that there is ample evidence to show that. In addition to forensic evidence, there is operative evidence for the following reason: This man was an Electroprivida driver, company driver, and he was waiting for someone outside of this restaurant, which kept on operating throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I do believe you.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I wasn't that sort of a police officer. I -- I didn't do operative work. There is probably material evidence to show that the man was killed there. I didn't find him there. But on account of the kind of injury that he had received, it was only to be expected that the witnesses would try to take him away from there and provide some medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're a scene of crime officer, aren't you? Wasn't the first thing you were ever taught to photograph the scene whenever you find someone who was killed? That is always the first thing do you in a murder investigation, right? First, you photograph the scene where a body was found and then you get on with the rest, because that shows whether the person was hit there or not, and we use the blood marks to show that, don't we? You were there to photograph the scene, so why did you not photograph the blood marks in that case?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I didn't photograph that and probably because I thought it was sufficient for me to have the blood marks inside the vehicle, and you do have that. That's part of the photo file. So that was probably the reason. I did not photograph the exact spot where the man fell to the ground, and I assumed the reason was because he did not actually die there, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying he died there. I'm saying that he fell to the ground right there. People came, people picked him, fetched him, took him away. He must have lost a lot of blood by this time. Why did you not photograph that place, that bit of ground where he fell?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that's because he didn't fall there, and he didn't die there but elsewhere. I photographed this vehicle with blood marks in which this man had been. I assumed that for the purposes of my evidence this was sufficient. That was probably the only reason I didn't actually photograph the very spot where the one fell to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You arrived the next day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you know where the vehicle had been parked on the previous day?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The vehicle had not been moved. It was always in the same place. And if you look at the marks on the vehicle, the sort of damage it had sustained, you immediately realise that the vehicle had been caught by the explosion. There were police officers securing the scene throughout the night. Those were my workmates. I came there; I asked no questions. I assumed when I arrive that the scene was intact; that it had properly secured. Did somebody move the vehicle or not, is not really something that I can say. As far as any evidence on the vehicle, there was nothing to lead me to believe that it had been moved. All the marks were fresh. The marks of the explosion, the blood marks were relatively fresh, and all of the other evidence that pointed to one conclusion that the vehicle had not been moved, as well as any other evidence. No dust moved around the vehicle itself, no dirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not photograph the path he took to the place where he eventually fell to the ground? It should have blood marks all along, right?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. As I told you, I didn't photograph the very spot he fell to the ground, but that doesn't mean there would have been a profusion of blood. As soon as he was wounded, he was put into this car and he was taken away, as Omar Masacic's [phoen] note indicates. I probably assumed at the time the about this place where the gentleman was hit and the blood marks, that my photographs were sufficient for my purposes, for the purpose of my report and my photo file.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, for this elucidation. It is now down to the Chamber to evaluate your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we have the other incident photograph, 65 ter 012019. The date is the 18th of July 1995. This is Prosecution Exhibit P236. If we could please have that document brought up for the witness's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in this, too? Did you say something about that a while ago, didn't you? The Prosecutor was showing you something about this, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The pages of 236 I exhibited were pages 2 to 6, if I'm not mistaken. That might help my friend Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you my learned friend that. That is indeed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was involved in the on-site investigation that led to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that so? When did you arrive on the scene in that case?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: We arrived at the scene. We took no more than five minutes to drive over in our Golf from the new Sarajevo police station. As a matter of fact, that was one of the most peaceful days throughout all the time that I was on duty in the station that I had been assigned to. I remember that we actually heard these four shells being fired, and we exchanged comments. I'm just trying to explain why we got there so fast. We were saying things like, they're shooting again, bullets flying again, and then our operation's duty officer, who was organising the whole team, told us that shells had landed on Velesici; and then the entire team present inside the police station at that moment packed our things and off we were to the scene as fast as we could, and then gentleman number 2 from Besera [phoen] joined us. We reached the scene with the shells landed within the shortest time possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And your absolutely positive that this came from positions held by the army of Republika Srpska, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: That's what was established, yes. That's what the investigation established, the on-site investigation. Gentleman number 4, the bomb squad technician, contributed that to the official report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what do you conclude where the shell had come from?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, we did the on-site work together. I did my job; he did his job. We investigated the scene of the explosion; and in this case, we were dealing with mortar shells, if I remember correctly. So the forensic technician determined where the projectiles had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us a number of times that it was normally not before the next day that you went to a crime scene simply because of the risk that the fire might continue, right?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how do you explain the fact that this time around it only took you five minutes, although the danger was sometimes there? How do you account for that fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I remember with great clarity that we took no long everybody than five minutes to get there, because we had the police car available. We did most of our work by walking; it was leg work. We had to walk to a scene. We got to this particular scene five minutes after we had been notified by the duty operation officer. Why did we get there so fast? Was I colleague scared? Was I scared? Having seen what I had seen there, I didn't even spend any time thinking. We just tried to get there as fast as we could. The firing had stopped after the shells landed and after that there was no more firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But how did you know? Five minutes later, how did you know that such atrocities had taken place there?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: We knew because the police station had its Velesici substation. This was called, if I'm not mistaken the police station number 3. We had one at Pofalici, that was police station numbering 2, and another in Hrasno, the Heroes Square, which was police station number 4. Our colleagues from the Velesici police substation informed us right away about this case. And I remember that when I was working on that earlier on-site investigation case, which was about 100 metres away from the other one - I think we had four incidents in a perimeter of some 100 metres - we got there information as we were working on this case. It was also probably due to their fast reaction. They secured the scene of crime, and we reached the place in fire minutes and were able to complete our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you didn't answer my question at all. Earlier on you avoided going out in to the scene of the crime immediately after the incident had taken place because you were afraid of the fire. In this particular instance, you were not fearful at all. You showed up there quite soon. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I will explain this. I told you about the incident on the 22nd of August and some other incidents where we were unable to attend the scene due to the ongoing shelling and sniping, but this applied only to these couple of incidents. We attended hundreds of scenes, and we would go out to the scene if it was possible. How would these things take place? Two or three rounds would be fired and then the situation would calm down. We would go out to the scene of the crime as soon as the circumstances permitted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What, in your view, should have happened then to prevent you from going there? You say, first, there was fire and then there was quiet. In your view, what should have followed after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stood sometime ago to just ask the parties, again, if we could move from a high speed down to some more reasonable gear. But I've been on my feet for about 25 seconds because things were going so fast the interpreter and the transcript had to catch up with everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the umpteenth time, you both speak the same language so it's natural to overlap, but you must observe a pause between question and answer. Mr. Tapuskovic, you have had experience with this before, so you should be setting the example for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the witness and Mr. Tapuskovic could wait for the transcript to be finished before they actually talk again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Although, I do not speak any English, that is the best method, and I will be mindful of that. But I don't know where we left it off now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you permit me, I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: You asked me what this "nothing" meant, what was I supposed to do? Well, when I said "nothing," this meant that, of course, I was not going to attend a scene of crime if I knew that I -- that a sniper had set the sites on me or that there was shelling going on. The highest price in my line of work was paid by police officers themselves who would come to the scene of the crime, to secure the scene, and would stand there until we reached the scene of crime. So when I said that after these shells landed, nothing happened, I meant that there was no more fire and we were able to attend the scene. This, however, did not mean that we could not have come under subsequent artillery fire and been injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: In every single case, you attended the scene of crime the day after. This was the only time when you reached the scene of the crime five minutes later, and you categorically state that you were there without actually knowing whether it was in fact secured.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I am categorically asserting that we were at the scene of the crime five minutes later. We knew there were casualties because the operations duty officer informed us to that effect. And we knew that the Velesici incident involved casualties. We reached the scene within five minutes in our official vehicle. The incidents that we have been referring to during my evidence here are not the only ones I worked on. I had other cases, and you can find that in my documentation, where I together with the bomb squad technicians attended scenes of crimes, very soon after the incidents happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about your colleagues? Were they right at the spot where the shells landed, so that's how you were able to join them there?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course not. Of course they weren't at the site of the impact. We had duty police officers from the Novo Sarajevo police station there. This was their patrolling area, as it were. As soon as the shells landed, residents reported that, just as they report burglaries today. Thus my colleagues were informed and they reached the site. Since the Velesici neighbourhood is quite a small area, I guessed there was a patrol making rounds who got word of the shelling incident and went there. They were informed of the shell landing and maybe even of the casualties involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's not clear to me where this line of question is leading. What is behind it? What is your purpose? Perhaps you should just put to the witness exactly what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be direct in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the reports and documents that I received only one or two days before your testimony, only on the 13th of February - and it took me quite some time to go through them - I may have overlooked it, but Witness, sir, I have not found anywhere in your documentation any information to the effect that you found blood marks at the scene of the crime, either you or your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: First of all, thanks to our prompt reaction we found dead people there. I recall that as soon as we reached the relevant street we found Mr. Zolata, that is to say, father and son dead there. In some other case, we found a man in his garden with his body ripped apart. You are asking me about finding bloodstains. Well, let me tell you that I found dead bodies at the scene of the crimes, and I believe that from my perspective, finding bodies is more relevant than bloodstains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Loss of life is always a terrible thing, but my question to you is: When you reached the scene of the crime, I put it to you that these people were killed elsewhere and that in a very short span of time you relocated these bodies and left them at these scenes. This is what I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are entitled, by virtue of your duty before this Tribunal, to put this to me, but let us take all the persons involved in drafting the reports; let us take the relatives of the persons killed or wounded in these incidents. These were neighbourhoods predominantly populated by Bosniaks, people living in individual family houses, not apartment blocks. Why don't you also put it to them that these dead bodies were taken from somewhere else and left at these scenes of crimes? I'm telling you that this is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We would all be better served if you just answer the question correctly, and you answered it. You say this is not the case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But where is the blood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would expect you to provide us with some assistance when you put to the witness that -- an allegation that these corpses were placed there by the witness or by somebody in the witness's unit. I would expect you to provide some sort of substance behind that allegation. Do you have any reason to believe that this was done, or can you, in any way, provide us with some evidence that this might have been the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I worked on some 300 murder cases in my career. When a person is killed, the first thing that ought to remain as a trace beneath his body are bloodstains. I will finish this line of questioning. However, let the witness first explain how it is possible for him to find a person on the spot where the person got killed without taking a photograph of the bloodstains left behind -- beneath the man's body. I am asking him to account for the missing piece of evidence. How is it possible for a forensics team to attend a scene of crime and not take such pictures whilst carrying a camera with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I fully respect your independence to cross-examine the way you see fit, but the indictment here and this particular charge is about the shelling. So I think the relevant part here would be whether you deny the shelling, in the first instance, because the fact of whether there were casualties as a consequence of the shelling perhaps is of lesser importance if we have first initially established that the shelling did take place. And this is what your client is accused of in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will never deny shelling or deny that life was lost. However, one ought to first establish whether shelling caused a person to lose his or her life. If the on-site investigation fails to show that there were any bloodstains, then how is it to be proven that a person was killed on the spot if the piece of evidence showing blood at the crime scene is not there? I am claiming, upon full responsibility because I know what the responsibility of a Defence lawyer is, that the bodies were indeed in the condition they were found in, but they were originally not at the crime scenes they were claimed to be. Any murder, to be proven, has to be substantiated with appropriate evidence. If a person was killed at a certain spot, then the first thing that has to be proven is that he indeed was killed on that very spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have gone through the document carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, where is the medical documentation attendant to the persons who were killed and wounded? Where is it? There is no medical documentation for any of the casualties, for not a single one, because based on the documentation I have here, one has no way of saying which way they got killed.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I will repeat: It was not my duty to take care of the medical documentation. It was the duty inspector who had to obtain medical documentation. I'm sure that medical documentation can be found somewhere in the file. As far as bloodstains are concerned, of which there has been a lot of discussion here, these photographs I believe do show persons who were killed as a result of shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have heard enough of this. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will even withdraw my questions with regard to two similar incidents. I have another document which was not used by the Prosecution, but it was listed under 65 ter as 01128. These are the events dated the 5th of July, 1995. This is a batch of documents that I included in my list of exhibits as soon as it was disclosed to me by the Prosecution. I did not ask for your leave to do this, but there it is, I did it. Can we call 65 ter document 01128 relating to the events of the 5th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this document dated 5th July 1995? Since I got this as part of the evidence accompanying your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry for the intervention, but the translation that appears on the screen isn't the document that appears in Serbo-Croatian on the screen. And I'm trying to do this by way of assistance, but I think if you go to page 4 you may see the original version of the translation that is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's either 3 or 4. As you've seen, Your Honours, my math isn't the best. It's a problem, we realise, when we're dealing with discreet documents from large investigative files, Your Honour, and we've been in contact with Mr. Registrar about how to fix this problem in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see, after this on-site investigation report of the 7th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We still don't have the English translation, but in the interests of time, let us proceed with the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well done. The English translation is of excerpts of the document, the B/C/S document, that appears on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand it. The layout is different, entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe I spoke again too quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, first we need to be sure that the B/C/S is the right one and then we'll search for the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Tapuskovic can indicate the page number that he wants in B/C/S and then we might be able to cross-reference the translation properly. At this point, Mr. Tapuskovic, if you give the ERN number, that would also help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 03307952 and 953, and the next one, 954. Then follows the criminal report against Radovan Karadzic, Ratko Mladic, and Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. We have the document that Mr. Tapuskovic wants. That's at page 16, and there is no translation of that document he's asked for. So we have the right B/C/S document that he wants and I hope we can move forward with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the document now, the one that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The B/C/S document is on the screen. It bears the ERN number Mr. Tapuskovic asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I got this document in relation to your testimony, in the certificate that is before you, it is said that: "Milutin Cevriz arrived at our institution on 5 July 1995, at 2000 hours. He is under reference number 276. The aforesaid person was injured by the explosion of a shell at the Square of Heroes/Trg Heroja." Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. That gentleman was, indeed, injured by a shell explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That happened on the 5th of July; correct? That incident that he recounted in which he was injured was on the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: From what I know, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that a time of very fierce fighting between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I would say that the summer of 1995 was the most intensive summer. Everybody knows that. 1995, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the offensive and the fighting in June and July that was very intensive and that there was fire from both sides?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I know that in the summer of 1995 Sarajevo, as a whole and the municipality I was in, was exposed to great shelling and sniping. I worked at the police. I had nothing to do with military activities and I know little about military activities. All I know is what happened in the Novo Sarajevo municipality in the summer of 1995, which was a period of intensive shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we move to page 2 of this document. 03307953. Can we turn to the next page, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this page?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We see the date here, and all the references here are about armed conflict. And next to all these names, let us look at, for instance, number 11, Milutin Cevriz, as a part of the total of 17 persons who were injured or killed in armed conflict, but next to each of these names we see the words "armed conflict," "armed conflict," "armed conflict." Can we assume that all of the people listed here were, in fact, casualties of that armed conflict that ranged that whole day, because we see a list of 17 people here. Next to each name it says "armed conflict," "armed conflict," "armed conflict." Were these people killed or wounded as part of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask my friend to put some context to this document. It has no heading; it has no information about location and, in fact, there is not a single name on this document that appears in any of the other the forensic investigative documents dealing with this incident. So perhaps if he could provide us with some further information, otherwise, Your Honours, it's just seems to be a question in the air. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. Lay a foundation, Mr. Tapuskovic. Avail yourself of the break for that purpose. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, was the month of July a period marked by intense fighting between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: As a forensic officer, I remember the month of July of 1995 as a very difficult period where the Novo Sarajevo municipality where I worked was under fire. Since I was a forensic officer and not a military person, I cannot testify about whether the period was marked by fierce fighting between the two armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I have before me is not the document that I obtained, but I got it from the OTP, and I said that this was 65 ter 01128. I was wrong in not numbering the pages of the document, and that was why it took us so long to find the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, according to the document that I received from the Prosecution, which you have now before you, the certificate before was dated the 30th of November. It is issued by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Institute for Urgent Medical documentation. According to this document, one person was killed on the 17th of July. And it is stated, with regard to 13 persons, that on the 2nd of July up to the 5th of July, all these persons were, in fact, wounded in that period. It is stated on what date they were wounded and at what time, and it is always indicated that they were wounded in the armed conflict. It doesn't say which armed conflict, and my question for you is: In your view, is this, in fact, the month that proved to be very difficult for you as well as the police force in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, now having heard the foundation and what this document purports to relate to, I would object to the question on the basis of relevance. It's the dealing with a time period and people who do not appear to be connected in any way to the incident that Mr. Hasanefendic is being cross-examined about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it is related to the period within the indictment, and we have had evidence concerning months in which there were very heavy casualties. I'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that I see in front of me is not something I'm aware of it. I don't know what this is about. Of all these names and if we could look at the bottom of the document, I'm only familiar with the person named Milutin Cevriz under number 11. This person, according to our knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness has said he doesn't know anything about the document and the only person he knows is Milutin Cevriz. Perhaps we should hear what you know about Milutin Cevriz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person was wounded in the -- in a shelling incident on which I worked. I investigated the case, together crime inspector and a bomb squad technician. He was a casualty at the Square of Heroes; and as far as we know, he was taken to the hospital and was wounded in -- whilst working, or rather, whilst attending to his garden. And that's the only thing I know about the person. I have him in my notes on the basis of the crime police inspector's notes who worked with eye-witnesses. I suppose that the document from the emergency ward is the document that was sent to the crime police inspector in order to complete his file. That is only thing I can tell you on the basis of his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You state that this gentleman, in this armed conflict that was intensive and happening every day, that this particular person died while attending his vegetable garden. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I claim that he was wounded in an area where there was this improvised garden of sorts, and I also said that it was a common occurrence of the time where people would plant their own vegetable gardens. They would also use the seeds that they received through humanitarian aid, and this was no uncommon occurrence. And on the Square of Heroes, Trg Heroja, there was a large green area where many people plant the their gardens. I cannot state this with certainty, but I suppose he was doing just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your statement that he himself was targeted, that a sniper, a member of the army of Republika Srpska, had set his sites particularly on him. Because you see on this list it is stated that all of the persons listed there were wounded during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I repeat that I don't know the document and why it says armed conflict and that the person was injured during the armed conflict. I absolutely stand by what I said, that the person was wounded in that area in this improvised garden. The Square of Heroes was shelled on a daily basis. Now, how his wounding came about, I don't know. I can only tell you that we investigated the impact, the shelling impact. The shell did not hit the ground. It hit the -- the fence of balcony there. There were people seated there, but they were only shell shocked. None of them were wounded. This gentleman was wounded by shrapnel that ricochetted against the balcony there. The gentleman was immediately taken to the emergency ward, and we didn't see him there, which was only natural. People would first be taken for treatment and only later would inspectors approach them to take their statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are, therefore, stating quite the opposite, that none of these persons were wounded as the result of the armed conflict taking place during that month?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: The only thing I'm claiming is with regard to Milutin Cevriz, there person listed here under number 11. I can tell you that he was wounded as a civilian in his garden on the Square of Heroes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your evidence on that point is clear. Next question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be marked for identification? I will probably try to collect other evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It already can come in as a exhibit in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But if you only want to have the marked for identification, then so be it. Do you want it as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reluctant to propose that, but in fact we would like to tender it as an exhibit. That's 65 ter 01128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D69, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is my friend referring to this page or is he referring to the whole file that is found at 65 ter number 1128?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should be this page. This page. Yes, the particular page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask my case manager to call on to our screens map P232.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you placed some markings on it, and with the red line you marked the area of responsibility of the army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I marked the area of responsibility of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as we see it, the area of responsibility of the army of Republika Srpska was surrounded on three sides by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: When we look at it in this image, then this is the case. But if we zoomed out, then the case would be quite the opposite. Do you get my meaning?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting. That is exactly my intention, to zoom out. The green area we see at the bottom of the map, which lies behind the area of responsibility, is that Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the green area to the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I marked the entire area of Grbavica 1 and 2; the entire area of Vrace Brdo, and the area leading to the Jewish cemetery, because Debelo Brdo is right behind the Jewish cemetery. Therefore, next to my red line where I marked the territory under the control of the Serb army, this should be to the right of that line. That's Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark Debelo Brdo for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In a different colour pen, if it isn't already, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in on the bottom right side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe the photograph is quite appropriate. Why would you like to us zoom in?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Because I wouldn't want to make a mistake. I know that Debelo Brdo is next to the Jewish cemetery, and believe me, I can't locate the Jewish cemetery on this image.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, given the issues about the clarity and the resolution in this image on the computer earlier on, I could propose that we move to the higher resolution picture that we have here that might assist the witness in his markings and to be able to identify features. He's just said he is unsure and doesn't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I disagree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I believe that since he has been working on this map he should continue working with it. Do your best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will do my best. Let us look at the original image that we had, because this has been zoomed in a bit. I need the entire photograph, just as we had it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't believe that we should proceed the way the witness wants.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my submission would be that if it's a matter of clarity and accuracy, and the witness has asserted he feels he can be more accurate with the picture presented to him in another format, that's exactly what we should be doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he asked for the entire photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend found this image quite clear at the time the witness was plotting certain matters into the marks. I find the image quite satisfactory. I want him now to plot in some blue lines next to the red lines that he had already marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness and Mr. Tapuskovic, we'll stick to the same photograph, the very same photograph. If the witness can't identify it and he says that he can't identify it, then so be it. The Chamber will assess it. So, Witness, it is for you to determine whether you wish to seek to identify it in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, can I just add that you can put another map to him or a better map, if you want to -- if you want to have the witness identify where Debelo Brdo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no better map for the matter in hand, with the lines already drawn. There is absolutely no better map. No map could possibly be better, especially since this is the same map that the Prosecutor used previously. All I wish to cross-examine the witness on is this particular map. Should that prove impossible, well, then, I wouldn't know what else to do. This map is perfect. It gives a great overview of all the important positions in the area. I really see no reason to seek a different map now and make things difficult for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on. We've been wasting time. As I told you, if you are unable to identify it, then say so and we'll move on. Just give us your reasons and it's for the Chamber to make an assessment of that, in light of the evidence. Are you in a position to identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. I'll oblige. I just thought it might be a good idea to get the resolution up a little bit, but this is no problem at all. The Debelo Brdo area is near the Jewish cemetery, which should be right here in this photograph, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just for clarity, have you identified the Jewish cemetery or have you identified Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have identified the Debelo Brdo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You do know, Witness, don't you, that the Jewish cemetery was not being held by the Serb forces alone. There were BH army units there, too. Please, can you indicate exactly where the Jewish cemetery is.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: That should be quite easy. The Jewish cemetery --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we do that are there two questions in sentence or is the only question as to the location of the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have asked two question, Mr. Tapuskovic. The first one was whether the witness knows that the Jewish cemetery was being held by the Serb forces alone. Witness, what is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the entire area of Jewish cemetery was under the control of the Serb forces. As for where exactly the confrontation line ran through the Jewish cemetery, that is not something that I can address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you to show us the Jewish cemetery first; pinpoint the location, please.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: All right. Number 4 means the Vrbanja bridge and the Jewish cemetery should be just passed the Vrbanja bridge, this area over here. So a little to the right. You can erase this blue circle here. So this circle should be further to the right and then it would end up encompassing the Jewish cemetery area. It is exactly between the Kovacici neighbourhood and Sol Kobuna [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, can we do that then? The witness has just asked to erase a blue circle and make a circle further to the right and then it would end up encompassing the Jewish cemetery area exactly between a certain neighborhood and Sol Kobuna. SO I think he has asked for a correction to be made on the map, which he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He didn't really ask for that. He said just said so this circle should be further to the right. So I took it that the evidence will be read in that way, but if you wish -- Witness, do you wish to have the circle moved further to the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I did ask for this circle to be erased, because I would like to have it moved a little to the right to encompass the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the exact location, the entire area of the Jewish cemetery should be to the right of the Vrbanja bridge, right here; more specifically, this entire area there. As to the confrontation line, I think it ran right through the Jewish cemetery, down the middle of the Jewish cemetery, but I never went there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At any rate, what you have just shown is the fact that the Jewish cemetery, for the most part, is in the territory covered by the BH army, maybe a very small portion of it remains in the territory under the control of the Serb forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: You see, we look at this red line that I drew on the right-hand side. That is precisely why I said I could use a bigger map, so that I could draw for you on a house-to-house basis what the Serb territory was and what the BH army territory was with greater accuracy. The Jewish cemetery - it's difficult to see - but I think it was right here in this area of responsibility. But the entire Jewish cemetery area was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Where was the confrontation line, I don't know exactly. I was no soldier myself. I was a forensic officer, a forensic technician. I wasn't even able to go there; only the military could. I don't want to be misunderstood on this. I'm not saying that the Jewish cemetery was in territory controlled by the BH army; that is definitely not true. If you want me to be more specific, get a bigger map. I'll draw the exact areas for you on a bigger map, if you like, and I will try to be as specific as I can. The entire area stretched from the Vrbanja bridge, across the Borak neighbourhood, and onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The drawings that you have been making throughout your evidence, are they not meant to be approximations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I said is this is the Jewish cemetery area, but it's very difficult to be positive about the confrontation line using this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, what you have just drawn for us shows that the Jewish cemetery was in territory covered by the BiH army. Only a small section of it is in territory covered by the army of Republika Srpska. It barely touches their territory. Could we say that, based on this image?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: What I said is I didn't know the exact confrontation line through the Jewish cemetery. I was not a member of the armed forces. I was never physically there. Jewish cemetery is an area which was crossed by the confrontation line. Truth to tell, I don't know how I find myself answering these questions since I was never there to begin with. Secondly, needless to say, I think the confrontation line was there. Obviously, part of the Jewish cemetery could have fallen under the BiH army and another part perhaps under the Serb forces. I don't know how line shifted, but I know that by and large the Jewish cemetery was under the control of the Serb army, as well as those streets over there, Trbelica Street and all those other streets. Those were under the control of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've marked the map, Witness, and we've heard this from several other witnesses. I'm about to ask you: Debelo Brdo was a BH army military position, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Again, I was not a member of the BH army; I was a member of the police. I never in my life set foot on Debelo Brdo. I am know longer sure how to try answering your question. Back in 1992 was Debelo Brdo under the control of the Serb forces or under the control of the BH army back in 1993? The simple answer is, I don't know. It wasn't my job to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Coming back to your personal details. You were born in Sarajevo on the 21st of January, 1975; yet you say that you never set foot on Debelo Brdo. Born and bred in Sarajevo, sir, can that be true?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: It is precisely for that reason that I ended up never going there. If you ask anybody else, anybody of Sarajevo's resident, there was no need. We would take trips to Jahorina, Bjelasnica, Trebevic. But beyond Trebevic, I never set foot on Debelo Brdo in my entire life, and something else before that. Before the war, I may not have been aware of the fact that it was called Debelo Brdo to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you stand in downtown Sarajevo, you can practically reach for it with your hand. I spent sometime there as a child. I remember that very clearly. Isn't it true that if you are somewhere from Marindvor, it is in the palm of your hand practically? The hill over looks the whole of Sarajevo, the whole downtown Sarajevo, for all practical intents.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: You're quite right, geographically speaking, that here it is clearly visibly. Before you war, I simply was not aware of its name. I didn't know it was called Debelo Brdo. I had never been there before or after. Most of Sarajevo's natives were probably more familiar with Hum and not with Debelo Brdo, but that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You marked that using number 6 and 7, and we'll be getting to that at a later stage. Can you tell me this, sir: Have you ever been to Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course I have. Mojmilo and Dobrinja, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about this ridge, Mojmilo. How long is it? Maybe you don't know. I know because I asked specifically. It's nearly three kilometres long the ridge, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I assume you mean Mojmilo hill, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I really have no idea how long it might be. You say three kilometres. I suppose you've double-checked. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand why you are reluctant to say anything very specific, but you marked this point as number 5 [as interpreted] and that was the position most severely affected by the shelling. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Number 5 was not Mojmilo according to the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that what Mr. Tapuskovic was putting? I thought he had moved away from that. What are you putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't saying that. I wasn't saying that number 5 was Mojmilo. What I was say is something that the witness had said in answer to one of the questions by the Prosecutor that the area marked as number 5 was a frequent target for the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I marked the Square of Heroes as number 5. This was a municipality, an area in Sarajevo, and this was most frequently targeted by the Serb shells and snipers. This was the former Perako Sanco [phoen] Square, and now it is called the Square of Heroes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you've said this, and now that you told us that you had been to Mojmilo, wouldn't Mojmilo be just opposite this area that you marked as number 5? The entire length of Mojmilo stretches just behind this area. Can you confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I'll put it like this. Behind this area, what we find is not Mojmilo but Hrasno hill, which stretches all the way to Lukavica. What you see behind the area marked as number 5 is Hrasno hill. Once you cross that hill, you reach the centre of Lukavica. Mojmilo hill is all the way to the left from this perspective, near the Mojmilo settlement or neighbourhood. What you see behind this area here is Hrasno Brdo, which is a really lovely hill, right there in Sarajevo. If you want me to, I can mark it for you. So I said this X above number 5, left from the football stadium Zelesnica is called Hrasno hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Here it is. All this is Hrasno hill. Now, if we would take a turn around the hill and went all around the hill, we would reach the centre of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is this: This hill, too, is an area where the ABiH was deployed, because it's in that area. That hill overlooks the area marked by 5.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: On that hill, on that hill called Hrasno, there also existed a demarcation line. People in Sarajevo know about streets, Milinklacka and Ozrenska, where a part of the hill near the stadium was also held by the Serb army throughout the war. I would particularly stress those streets, Milinklacka and Ozrenska street. That is to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you to confirm again, because I think you've already confirmed it, that this hill, Hrasno, was held, according to the red line you have already marked, by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I'll have to say this again: There was a demarcation line on that hill as well. One part of the hill was held by the BH army; the other part of the hill was held by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now show us where this demarcation line was.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: From what I know, through my job in the police and through all the information that was available to me, at the stadium that we see here there was nobody. It was a clear area. And where exactly this demarcation line ran, I think it ran just above the Zelesnica football stadium, but through which streets I really don't know. But that's where the demarcation line was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did it run through Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja is 7 kilometres away from the area we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but if we want to reach Lukavica, this top of the hill was held by the BH army, the one that you marked with the cross.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether the BH army held the top of the hill. I've never been there. I know approximately where the demarcation line ran; above the football stadium, across the Samac hill. But what was exactly held by the BH army, you would have to ask somebody from the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who held Samac hill?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think that the demarcation line ran even through the Samac or Sarac hill, but that's not something that I can confirm. You would have to ask somebody who was in the BH army or possibly the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And further there is the ridge of Mojmilo, to the left.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, you would have to go left. But before you reach Mojmilo, you have to go across two other hills. Public transportation goes across those hills, Svrakina Selo and Aneks. There are some private houses there, family houses. If you say that it was 3 kilometres long, it sounds like an exaggeration to me. But that's where Mojmilo is, quite far from this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But all these three hills that you mentioned were in the area of responsibility of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Hrasno hill was in the areas of responsibility of both the BH army and the Serb army; I'm saying this for the third time. The demarcation line ran through Hrasno. Debelo Brdo, to the best my knowledge, was under the control of the Serb army at the beginning of the war, and I'm hearing from you for the first time now that maybe the BH army held part of it. Maybe there was a demarcation line there as well. And Vrace hill was definitely under the control of the Serb army. There are the villages of Petrovici, Milivici, in that vicinity; they were definitely under the control of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I did not ask you about the situation at the beginning of the war. I'm asking you about the time for which Dragomir Milosevic was indicted, which was August 1994, and I'm taking you back to this hill again. Even there was a demarcation line running through it, the top of the hill was held by the BH army - and that's what I'm putting to you - and all these hills, all the way to the end, all the hills you enumerated, were under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: As for the top of Hrasno hill, I really don't know. I cannot answer that question. You have to understand that only army people had access to that area. I don't know where the demarcation line ran through Debelo Brdo. Aneksi and Strakina Selo were, indeed, under the BH army control and the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for Hrasno, I know that part of it was held by ABiH and another part by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And all the other hills we mentioned were held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Svrakino Selo, Aneks, Mojmilo, Velesici, Pofalici that you see under number 6 and 7. Those are the hills covered by populated areas. People live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to take much more of the Trial Chamber's time. This area under 6 and 7, all this was under the control of the BH army, including Hum, Zuc, and a number of other hills, all of them higher than 800 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. Once again, I think there is a couple of questions actually in this that perhaps are best answered separately or put to the witness separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is: The area under 6 and 7 was under the control of the BH army, including Hum, Zuc, and a number of other hills, all of them higher than 800 metres. If you want to separate that, then you could answer the first one. Were they under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I think that implies that Hum and Zuc were in the areas marked as 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the areas that I marked with 6 and 7, Velesici, Pofalici, and the hill Hum in the continuation of that line, were indeed under the control of the BH army. There was fierce fighting at Zuc. Whether the BH army controlled Zuc, I don't know, and I don't know up to where they controlled it. I know they controlled one part. And in conclusion, I'm not aware that these hills are higher than 800 metres, because I never checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There was fighting around Zuc, but in 1992. However, in 1994 and 1995, it was only BH army forces that were concentrated there and they controlled the entire Sarajevo from that side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: On Zuc hill, I don't know what kind of positions the BH army held and what positions were held by the Serb army. I know Zuc hill was characterised by fierce fighting, but I really don't know where the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was, although I was never their member and I never visited those demarcation lines. There were only members of BH army units who had proper military service books and who were assigned there. I worked in the forensic department of the Ministry of the Interior in the Security Services of the Novo Sarajevo municipality, and my policeman's job never took me to the trenches at Hrasno, Zuc, or anyone where else. I really cannot provide with you any information about the positions of military forces at Zuc and Hrasno hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, in conclusion, what we see on this map, from this side of the red line until the top of the map, was it all under the BH army control?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: What we see on this picture, this area, it's not the entire municipality of Novo Sarajevo. As I said at the beginning of my testimony, it is only a part of Novo Sarajevo. And what we see and what I marked above the red line, as you say, was entirely under the control of the BH army. But if you went further down, it was no longer under the BH army control. This depicts only part of Novo Sarajevo municipality. Hrasno, Pofalici, Velesici, Marshal Tito Barracks, Vrace hill, and towards the centre towards Marindvor. We don't see Dolac-Malta. We don't see all of Pofalici, which divides into upper and lower. We don't see all of Velesici either. What we see on this photograph above the red line, that was indeed under BH army control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want it deal with this map any longer, but turn around to face this large map here. First, look at the centre where it says, "1st Corps. " Right, in that blue circle. Were all the hills within that circle under the control -- were they all under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I would really have to approach the map to look carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness as reiterated and re-reiterated that his job in the police force didn't take him to the front lines. How on earth could be in a position to say which hills or elevations were under the control of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's for him to say. Are you in a position to do what you're being asked by counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the fourth time I'm saying it. I worked in the forensic department of the police, and what the esteemed counsel is asking me is something that I cannot answer with any certainty. Where were the demarcations lines? Where were the positions of BH army? If you find a witness, who was earlier a member of the BH army, he will certainly be able to tell you. As for residential areas and Novo Sarajevo where I worked as a scene of crime officer and I went out into the field, that is something that I can speak about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In those circumstances, the proper course is for you to say -- for you to decline to say to answer, to say you're not in a position to say. And that's the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. But I have said it four times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you have not said it with sufficient clarity, because you have gone on to identify on several occasions various locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke of locations where I visited and moved around as a scene of crime officer, but I always stated for the record that I never went to the demarcation line between the BH army and the VRS. The areas where I was able to move and where I conducted on-site investigations are areas that I'm familiar with. I don't know about any other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: More on to another area of questioning, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As a police inspector and a native of Sarajevo, do you know where Butmir airport is? Can you at least show us Butmir airport on the map behind you.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course I know where Butmir airport is. Butmir airport is in the so-called airport neighbourhood next to Dobrinja, but that was not my area of work. I think it belongs to Ilidza municipality or perhaps Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show it on this map behind you.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I'll try, although I've never seen this map before, but I will try to locate Butmir airport. Here, in this area, is where it should be. But we can't really see it because it's covered by red. That's where the airport is. I've just shown where Butmir airport in Sarajevo is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that next to the airport at this point in time, the time we're talking about, August 1994, November 1995, there was a tunnel that was used? Is this something that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course I am. Anyone from Sarajevo knew about that. This was a tunnel that was Sarajevo's only link to the outside world. I personally never crossed that tunnel. I can confirm that I was familiar with its existence, as anyone would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that every day battalions passed through that tunnel, BH army battalions, on their way in from Herzegovina? On their missions, they would leave, they would go on other missions, and then take the same tunnel back into Sarajevo. Are you familiar with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never took the tunnel myself. I have no information to indicate whether it was used by the army or not. How frequently it was used and by how many soldiers specifically, I don't know. I spent most of the war, most of the time in 1994 and 1995, in Sarajevo municipality, Novo Sarajevo municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the downtown area. I never ventured that far throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In chief, you testified that you never saw a single heavy weapon in Sarajevo, didn't you, or anything else with the possible exception of rifles and pistols? Did you see any heavy weapons deployed inside Sarajevo, sir?

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: As far as my experience goes, I stand by my previous answer which was in relation to mortars. I never saw any mortars or heavy weapons in Sarajevo. What did I see? Light automatic weapons and several police APCs. Quite rarely, though. Therefore, I can say that I never laid eyes on any form of heavy weapons inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, on page 138, line 9, the witness was never asked in chief whether he saw heavy weapons in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Mr. Tapuskovic, you should be coming to the end of your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely my intention. I had lots of documents that I was going to use, but I've decided to drop most of them. The next document, DD00-0757, that's my next document, the one that I've got lined up for the witness. It's a document that I obtained from the BH archive. Before I come to grips with that, I would like to ask the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If the police, that is, his own units and primarily the Bosna unit, had any serious weapons. I'm saying "serious weapons" in order not to exaggerate.

utterances.speaker: SANJIN HASANEFENDIC
utterances.text: I can say that in my own police station the crime squad people had their pistols, their official weapons that they signed for.
